The snow crab Chionoecetes opilio exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in its ultimate body dimensions, with females attaining a maximum carapace width of 9.5 centimeters [Li = 9.5 centimeters], while males reach a substantially larger ultimate carapace width of 16.5 centimeters [Li = 16.5 centimeters]. This divergence in adult size reflects the species' mating system, in which larger males secure preferential access to ovigerous females during reproductive pairing. At the onset of independent life, newly hatched zoea larvae emerge from incubating eggs with an extremely modest wet weight at birth of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a value derived from the typical egg dimensions observed in related majoid crabs. These free-swimming larvae drift in the water column as planktonic crustacean larvae, gradually growing through successive nauplius stages before undergoing the dramatic body plan reorganisation known as larval metamorphosis. The duration of this pelagic phase is strongly temperature-dependent; at the warmer conditions typical of surface waters, estimated at approximately 8 °C [T = 8 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis has been measured at roughly 152.5 days .

Subsequent to larval metamorphosis and benthic settlement, the post-metamorphic juveniles enter a period of rapid somatic growth on the seafloor. For male snow crabs, the onset of sexual maturation is signalled by the attainment of a specific carapace width at puberty for males of 3.9 centimeters [Lp = 3.9 centimeters]. This morphological threshold coincides with a considerable increase in body mass; males reaching this pubertal moult exhibit a wet weight at puberty for males of 29.7 grams [Wwp = 29.7 grams]. The duration of the developmental interval from the moment of benthic settlement to this reproductive activation is approximately 1460 days following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 1460 days following metamorphosis], a period of four full years under the cold conditions prevailing in their deep at a temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C]-water habitat. During this prolonged juvenile phase, the crabs must accumulate sufficient lipid reserves to sustain the physiological demands of gonad maturation and the energetic costs of the eventual pubertal ecdysis event.

Reproductive output in snow crab is tightly constrained by the cold temperatures characteristic of their continental shelf and slope habitats. Under the cold conditions typical of their continental shelf and slope habitats, maintained at a stable temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is reflected in a spawning event yielding approximately 150,000 eggs per spawning [N_R_i = approximately 150,000 eggs per spawning] and an annual spawning frequency of about 1 spawning per year [F_R_i = about 1 spawning per year]. At the same thermal regime of 5 °C [T = 5 °C], the age at birth, representing the incubation duration from gamete fusion to the emergence of the first zoeal larval stage, has been documented as 365 days [ab = 365 days]. This extended incubation period, lasting a full calendar year, is a direct consequence of the slowed metabolic and developmental rates imposed by near-freezing bottom temperatures, and is consistent with the prolonged embryogenesis observed in other cold-water lithodid and oregonid crabs.

The life-history schedule of Chionoecetes opilio is notable for its extreme longevity relative to many other decapod crustaceans. Field-based mark-recapture studies and analysis of size-frequency distributions have yielded a maximum lifespan of approximately 6935 days [am = approximately 6935 days], which equates to roughly 19 years under the prevailing thermal conditions of 5 °C [T = 5 °C]. Achieving such a protracted existence requires the progressive accumulation of somatic tissue over many intermoult periods, culminating in the ultimate wet weight for males of 2250 grams [Wwi = 2250 grams] and the ultimate wet weight for females of 429.4 grams [Wwi = 429.4 grams]. The dramatic disparity in asymptotic mass between the sexes aligns with the selective pressures of male-male competition for access to berried females; larger males are disproportionately represented among mating pairs. Among females, the cessation of growth at a smaller size likely reflects the energetic demands of repeated egg production over successive years.

During the planktonic larval phase, newly metamorphosed individuals that have completed the megalopa stage weigh approximately 0.016 grams  at the moment of benthic settlement. The carapace length at settle measured at this critical transition from a pelagic to a benthic existence is 0.319 centimeters , a dimension that marks the initiation of the juvenile benthic phase. For male snow crabs, the interval from the larval-juvenile transition to the puberty moult spans approximately 1460 days post-settlement [tp = approximately 1460 days post-settlement], a figure that mirrors the general duration recorded for both at a temperature of 5 °C [T = 5 °C]sexes combined. Comparative analysis with congeneric species such as Chionoecetes bairdi suggests that these developmental timelines are broadly similar across the genus, though subtle differences in thermal optima may produce local variation. The slow growth and delayed maturity characteristic of C. opilio render it particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, as harvested males typically have had only limited opportunities to reproduce before reaching legal capture size.
